blocks.text: Whose vulture will this carcass be? [col. 310] [III, 64] I add one thing: instead of רחם racham, in Deuteronomy we read רחמה rachama, with a feminine ending. For I do not agree with those who hold that the He in רחמה is paragogic, since I know that in Arabic too the feminine رخمة [rakhama] rachama occurs far more often than the masculine رخم [rakham] racham. And, as Damir notes, الها فيها للجنس [al-hā fīhā li-l-jins] in that word the letter He pertains to the genus, lest it be thought to be the He of unity, as commonly among the Arabs. But, what is more surprising, although in Greek one says ὁ γὺψ [ho gyps] in the masculine gender, yet in the Greek version of Horapollo, an Egyptian writer, ἡ γύψ [hē gyps] is always read, evidently so that the Greek word should correspond to the Egyptian רחמה rachama, or to another word analogous to it, which was feminine. This seems to have arisen from a popular error, since most Egyptians were persuaded that all vultures are female, and that they conceive in no other way than by facing the south wind, or the east wind, when it blows. Horus, Hieroglyphica, book 1, chapter 11: Ἄῤῥεν ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ ὑπάρχει [Arrhen en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei], In this kind of animal there is no male. And after relating that other birds conceive from the wind eggs fit only for eating, not also for generation, he says: Γυπῶν δὲ οὐχ' ὑπηνέμιον ποιουμένων τὴν ὀχείαν ἡ τῶν ὠῶν γένεσις ζωογονεῖται [Gypōn de ouch hypēnemion poioumenōn tēn ocheian hē tōn ōōn genesis zōogoneitai], But in vultures, although they make a wind-borne union (that is, although they conceive in no other way than from the wind: for instead of οὐχ [ouch] I read κἂν [kan], or εἰ καὶ [ei kai], or something of the kind), a living creature is nevertheless generated from their eggs. Plutarch in the Roman Questions, Question 93: Εἰ δὲ (ὡς Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογοῦσι) θῆλυ πᾶν τὸ γένος ἐστὶ καὶ κυΐσκονται δεχόμενοι καταπνέοντα τὸν Ἀπηλιώτην· [Ei de (hōs Aigyptioi mythologousi) thēly pan to genos esti kai kyiskontai dechomenoi katapneonta ton Apēliōtēn] If it is true, as the Egyptians relate, that the whole race of vultures is female, and that they conceive by receiving the blast of the east wind. Ammianus, book 17, on the Egyptians: By the vulture they express the word for nature, because natural science records that no males can be found among these birds. Perhaps instead of naturae [nature] we should read matris [mother], as in Homer: Μητέρα δὲ γράφοντες γῦπα ζωγραφοῦσι, ἐπειδὴ ἄῤῥην ἐν τούτῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ζώων οὐχ' ὑπάρχει [Mētera de graphontes gypa zōgraphousi, epeidē arrhēn en toutō tō genei tōn zōōn ouch hyparchei]. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 12, History 439, after relating this very thing much more fully, declares that he drew it ἐξ Αἰγυπτίων [ex Aigyptiōn], from the Egyptians. This fable, then, first arose in Egypt; from there it gradually spread to the other nations, especially after the birth of Christ, since many doctors of the church eagerly embraced it, or at least used it as an argumentum ad hominem, as they call it, against those who denied that Christ could have been born of a virgin. Accordingly, that female vultures conceive and bear without intercourse is written, from the choir of the Fathers, by Tertullian against the Valentinians, chapter 10; Origen against Celsus, book 1; Basil on the Hexaemeron, book 5, chapter 20; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, page 27; Procopius on Isaiah; Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7. To these may be added Theophylact Simocatta, Physical Question 8; Philes, and Pisides in the Iambics (which others attribute to Cyril of Alexandria); Peter Damian, book 2, Letter 18; Tzetzes, as above; the Etymologicum, [III, 65] Cyril the lexicographer, the Scholiasts whom we have cited, etc. Nor do I doubt that this opinion, however false and absurd, already prevailed among many from the time of Moses. Far be it from us, however, to think that Moses, swept away by that torrent, ever imagined any such thing about the vulture, even in a dream. I mean only this: that in Deu- [col. 311] teronomy he used the feminine word רחמה rachama in order to speak with the common people. But, lest anyone should turn this into a defence of the error, in Exodus he said רחם racham in the masculine.
